articles.title: Lane Kiffin takes the side exit as Tennessee sends LSU home and moves to the doorstep of CFP
articles.summary: Tennessee football fans threw golf balls onto the Neyland Stadium field as Lane Kiffin and LSU exited early, with the Vols now one win from the CFP.
articles.body: KNOXVILLE, Tenn. — Lane Kiffin took the side exit. Tennessee took another step toward the College Football Playoff on Saturday night. On a night when golf balls again landed on the field at Neyland Stadium, the Volunteers beat LSU 27-13 to move within one win of a likely postseason berth. The closing minutes turned ugly as students threw items onto the playing surface, prompting LSU players to move toward midfield while police worked to restore order. CFP SELECTION COMMITTEE 'EXPLAINS' ITS LACK OF TRANSPARENCY: ISN'T REALLY 'FEASIBLE' | IAN MILLER Kiffin and the Tigers eventually left through a side exit, heading home with their fifth loss of a season that began with championship expectations. Tennessee, meanwhile, had plenty to celebrate. On the same day Indiana and UCLA lost on the road, the Vols strengthened their playoff case with a defense that forced three turnovers, held LSU to 265 total yards and fed off a crowd that helped cause seven false-start penalties. The 27-13 win over LSU should garner the Vols a number of points from the members that sit inside a gigantic room in Grapevine, Texas, looking at the "metrics." Should that performance push Tennessee ahead of an Alabama team that played an FCS opponent Saturday? There’s certainly an argument for it, especially since the Vols already beat the Crimson Tide in Knoxville. Will it? Given the committee’s affection for Alabama, don’t count on it. For Josh Heupel, the more useful calculation is simple: Beat Vanderbilt next week, and Tennessee will be packing for the playoff, after securing a must-win against an LSU team overloading with expensive talent. It was also in the same venue that hosted Lane Kiffin's return to Knoxville, which was met with a plethora of f-bombs dropped throughout the game. Who would of thought at the beginning of this season, with LSU marching into the year as one of the most talked about teams in all of college football, that the Tigers would be suffering their fifth loss of 2026. Tennessee finds a way to beat teams down, especially at home The former Vols coach heard plenty from a Neyland Stadium crowd that hasn’t forgotten his one season in Knoxville. The expletives were predictable. So was the attention surrounding his return, even if he has stood on the visiting sideline here before. But the football story belonged to Tennessee. The Vols leaned on the formula that has carried them through the season: DeSean Bishop and the running game, a defense capable of taking over, and enough timely plays to finish the job. It hasn’t always been pretty. It has been effective. 13TH-RANKED TENNESSEE DISMANTLES SIXTH-RANKED KENTUCKY TO STAY ALIVE IN COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF RACE Even though Lane Kiffin was making his return to Knoxville, which has happened more times than you think, he was back on the sidelines coaching a different team inside a stadium he roamed the sidelines on. The problem for the LSU head coach was that this story was not about him, at least this time. No matter what took place over the last five minutes of this game, the story is about Tennessee being one-game closer to reserving its spot in the CFP. Heck, you could make the argument that the Vols could afford another loss after the wild day that saw both Indiana and UCLA lose. But, it doesn’t help that their final game of the regular season will come against Vanderbilt, which doesn’t help much with strength of schedule. That's why, as Tennessee fans celebrated in the stands with "Dixieland Delight" following the win, you knew how important this game was for the program. CFP HANGOVER: INDIANA CAN’T ESCAPE SCHEDULE DEBATE, BUT ALABAMA GETS TO SKIP THE CONVERSATION ONCE AGAIN Was it the most critical game in the past decade? That's up for debate, even though there hasn’t been a game with these type of CFP implications in Knoxville. "It's a different style that maybe I've played. Maybe the old times folks would appreciate the style of play. We've played field position more than I have before, but winning in all three phases of the game," Josh Heupel said postgame about the CFP committee. Whether it's Faizon Brandon or George MacIntyre, the Vols found a way to use both quarterbacks against an LSU team known for its pressure on defense. What to make of this Tennessee team? They find ways to win Was it perfect? Nope. But, the Vols did rush for over 200 yards against an LSU team that has shined in that department throughout the season. You might not like the way this football team is winning games. That's fine, by the way. But, you cannot deny that they are finding different ways to win these types of games. Also, they have done it with the weight of the world bearing down on them. Nothing about this game from an offensive standpoint will be etched in the history books, and nor should it. But, against a team that has $43 million worth of talent on its roster, it was Tennessee's inept offense that put together two touchdowns and a defense with crucial stops in the fourth quarter that led to them being one win away from the postseason. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP You can say Tennessee doesn’t deserve to be ahead of Alabama, given that argument doesn’t seem to be going anywhere anytime soon. But, you can't tell me they aren’t in the same "pod" any longer after the win over LSU. Both teams defeated Lane Kiffin, and it was Tennessee beating Alabama this season in Knoxville. Maybe it doesn’t matter any longer, given the results that took place within the Big Ten on Saturday. But at the expense of Lane Kiffin and the LSU Tigers, it's Tennessee that found another gear in the fourth quarter that sent the former Vols coach back to Baton Rouge to deal with an upset fan base. As for Josh Heupel and the Vols, a trip to Nashville next week after Thanksgiving should turn into a CFP welcoming party.

articles.title: Iran says 428 children killed in two wars, Red Crescent chief calls for independent probe into Minab school attack
articles.summary: At least 428 children were killed during two wars involving Iran in June 2025 and February-April 2026, according to figures cited by Iranian Red Crescent
articles.body: At least 428 children were killed during two wars involving Iran in June 2025 and February-April 2026, according to figures cited by Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) President Pirhossein Kolivand, who has called for an independent investigation into the attack on a school in Minab and other reported incidents.Speaking on the occasion of World Children's Day on November 20, Kolivand said the protection of children during armed conflicts was not only a moral obligation but also a legal duty and a shared responsibility of all states and parties involved in conflicts.Citing reports on child casualties, he said at least 45 children and adolescents were killed during the 12-day war in June 2025, according to the Hengaw Organization for Human Rights."Furthermore, according to a letter sent by the Secretary of the Iranian Judiciary's High Council for Human Rights to the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), 383 children were killed and 2,115 others were injured during the 40-day war in Esfand 1404 and Farvardin 1405 [February–April 2026]."Kolivand said the figures indicated that at least 428 children had been killed in the two conflicts. He added that seven of the children killed during the second war were less than a year old.He said families continued to deal with the loss of children and the physical, psychological and social consequences of injuries sustained during the conflicts.Iran calls for independent probe into Minab school attackKolivand described the attack on Shajareh Tayyebeh School in Minab as one of the most tragic incidents during the period. Referring to a report by the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, he said 168 people, including students, teachers, school staff and some of their relatives, were killed in the incident.He called for the circumstances surrounding the attack to be established and those responsible to be held accountable."Schools are protected under international humanitarian law as long as they retain their civilian character. Attacks against them, in the absence of the necessary legal conditions, may constitute violations of the rules governing the protection of civilian objects," he stated.Kolivand said the families of the victims and the public were entitled to transparent and documented information about the incident, including how the decision to carry out the attack was made. He called for an independent and effective investigation.Red Crescent chief cites international humanitarian lawExplaining the obligations of parties involved in armed conflicts, Kolivand referred to the principle of distinction under international humanitarian law. It requires parties to distinguish between civilians and combatants, as well as civilian objects and military objectives.He said direct attacks on civilians and civilian objects were prohibited and that attacks must be directed exclusively at military objectives.Kolivand also referred to the principle of proportionality, which requires parties to assess the expected harm to civilians against the anticipated military advantage."Compliance with the principle of proportionality requires parties to armed conflicts to refrain from any attack expected to cause civilian deaths, injuries or damage to civilian objects that would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated."He added that parties to conflicts were also required to take all feasible precautions to prevent or minimise harm to civilians and civilian infrastructure.Kolivand said children were entitled to special protection under international humanitarian law and the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Their rights to life, health, education and care, he said, must be protected during armed conflicts.He also stressed that schools must remain safe environments for children's education and development and should be protected from attacks that violate international humanitarian law.Calls for accountability and support for affected childrenExpressing sorrow over the deaths and injuries of children and other civilians in attacks attributed to Israel and the United States against Iran, Kolivand condemned what he described as violations of international humanitarian law.He urged competent international bodies to investigate the attack on Shajareh Tayyebeh School and other reported incidents, following the principles of independence, impartiality and transparency, and to make their findings public.He also called for legal responsibility to be established, those found responsible to be held accountable under applicable legal standards, and compensation to be provided to victims and their families.Kolivand urged UNICEF and other international organisations to coordinate assistance for children affected by armed conflicts, including medical treatment, physical and psychological rehabilitation, psychosocial support and access to education."Support for children affected by armed conflicts must not be limited to emergency and short-term measures. It must also encompass their safe and sustainable return to normal life and the full enjoyment of their fundamental rights," he stressed.November 20 marks the anniversary of the United Nations General Assembly's adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989. Kolivand said World Children's Day was an opportunity to reaffirm the international community's responsibility to protect children's rights, particularly during wars and armed conflicts.He paid tribute to families who had lost children and those caring for children affected by the conflicts, and reaffirmed his commitment to pursuing truth, justice and accountability and defending children's rights to life, security, health and education.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: COP31 climate talks on the brink as new draft deal faces scrutiny
articles.summary: New draft would acknowledge for the first time that global ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠warming is on course to pass the 1.5C threshold.
articles.body:
The fate of United Nations climate talks in Turkiye is hanging in the balance as the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) co-presidents, Australia and Turkiye, struggle to secure consensus on a deal to advance the fight against climate change, raising ⁠⁠the prospect of no deal being reached.

The new draft of the deal was released on Sunday, two days after the conference in Antalya was scheduled to end.

If approved, it would acknowledge for the first time that global ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠warming is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold that countries had sought to preserve, while calling for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse the overshoot.

The draft omits mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say are driving climate change, an issue that has been at the centre of frictions at the talks. Instead, it includes language referring to ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌a previous COP at which governments had agreed to transition away from oil, gas and coal.

“We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon,” COP31 President Murat Kurum told a plenary session early on Sunday.

Kurum, who is also Turkiye’s environment minister, said the conference would reconvene later on Sunday morning to approve the deal.

Other delegations at the venue, where catering outlets and exhibits have already been dismantled, were less sure.

French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said the proposal was a “backward” step. “Time is ticking and we are not there yet,” she said.

An earlier draft had provoked strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels, the largest contributors to climate change.

Environmental group 350.org said it was disappointed by the continued omission in the new draft, as well as its encouragement of carbon-removal technologies.

“Carbon capture is one of the biggest scams of the overshoot era and our leaders are on ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠the verge of falling for it,” said Sara Shaw, the group’s campaigns and networks ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠director, referring to the practice of trapping carbon dioxide before it reaches the atmosphere.

Observers at the closed-door talks said Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing nations had pushed hard to keep fossil fuels out of the ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠text and carbon removal in.

A representative of the Saudi delegation declined to comment.

Kurum said he ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠believed concerns around fossil fuels had ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌been addressed, as had those ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌around helping developing countries finance their adaptation to climate change.

The new ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌text followed intensive consultations between Australia, which is ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌leading the talks; Turkiye, which is hosting the meeting; and nearly 200 delegations from many of the world’s richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations.

The summit’s agreement is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heatwaves, floods and other disasters.

An opening draft from Australia on Monday called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A slimmer version on Thursday removed every mention of them after Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers objected.

Key issues that slowed the agreement included how much effort countries should make to wean themselves off fossil fuels, such as coal, oil and gas.

Other issues included whether to encourage industrial carbon capture and storage of pollutants, as well as whether ramping up electricity generation should only be done with renewables, such as wind and solar, or also involve other sources such as natural gas and coal.

To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions.

The two-week talks in the Turkish city were due to end on Friday.

In a letter sent on Saturday to this year’s cohosts, Turkiye and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs” the UN has ever held.

The letter stated there were only hours left “to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations”.

In the lead-up to these talks, the UN said the world would likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial temperatures.

articles.title: Displaced Darfur families face volatile winter as Sudan aid cuts bite
articles.summary: Sudan’s displacement crisis could worsen with winter approaching.
articles.body:
Omdurman, Sudan – When Fatima Mohamed Haroun was displaced from West Darfur state at the start of Sudan’s war in 2023, she never imagined she would find herself caring for four of her grandchildren far from her home.

Haroun, who believes she is aged about 60, said her son went missing a year ago. His wife died after giving birth, leaving Haroun as the sole guardian of her four grandchildren.

Now living in a crumbling mudbrick building in al-Ghadir, north of Omdurman, in Khartoum state, she has received no humanitarian assistance since her displacement.

Without an income, it is only the goodwill of her neighbours that prevents Haroun and her grandchildren from starving. But every day is a battle to find food, water or medicine, and with winter fast approaching, proper shelter, warm clothes, and blankets for the children are another priority.

“I cannot work or earn money, so we depend on neighbours who occasionally give us food. But even our neighbours sometimes have nothing to eat. When they have no food, my grandchildren and I go to bed hungry,” she told Al Jazeera.

“We have no supplies to help us cope with the cold, not even blankets to keep us warm. We sleep on the ground with only the sky above us. The cold is severe, and the children are suffering. We appeal to the government and humanitarian organisations to provide food, blankets, covers and other basic necessities to help us endure the cold and protect our children.”

Temperatures can drop significantly in Omdurman during the winter, and at night al-Ghadir can be particularly cold due to its location close to mountainous areas. Displaced families living in temporary shelters here are especially vulnerable because they lack blankets, winter clothing and heating facilities.

The war in Sudan, which broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary in April 2023, has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

Khartoum state, which was initially one of the epicentres of the war but is now relatively more stable, continues to host large numbers of people forced to flee their homes, particularly from southern and western Sudan where fighting is ongoing. Millions of people in areas such as Darfur have experienced or are at risk of horrific violence, forcing them to flee to other parts of Sudan or neighbouring countries where they live in horrendous conditions.

As of July 30, Khartoum state was hosting 414,252 internally displaced people, according to data from the International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM).

Winter is expected to worsen conditions for families living in temporary shelters or unfinished buildings without adequate blankets and warm clothing.

Sudan has more than 8.5 million internally displaced people, according to DTM Sudan, with the IOM and the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) warning that millions are still without a roof over their heads and risk losing access to emergency shelters due to funding shortages .

About 15.4 million people in Sudan need emergency shelter and basic household items. The agencies said funding shortages mean humanitarian organisations can prioritise assistance for only 10 percent of those in need, leaving millions without support.

Fighting, general insecurity, drone attacks on civilian infrastructure and camps, as well as other logistical challenges were all obstructing aid deliveries, the agencies said. Less than half of the funding for Sudan’s 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which requires $2.9bn to assist 20.4 million people in need, had been received, forcing humanitarian agencies to scale back some services.

Abdelaziz Suleiman Ori, director of culture and information for the Darfur regional government, said his administration was monitoring the conditions for displaced people in host states, including Khartoum, and coordinating humanitarian assistance.

The regional government has drawn up a winter plan that includes blankets, clothing and food to respond to the impending crisis, but Ori acknowledged that available resources were so far insufficient.

“Since the outbreak of the war on April 15, Governor Minni Arko Minawi has dispatched humanitarian convoys from Port Sudan to el-Fasher, passing through Madani, Kosti and El Obeid. We are also in contact with international organisations and UN agencies to monitor the situation of displaced people in different states,” Ori told Al Jazeera.

“Our winter plan includes blankets, clothing, food and children’s necessities. But our resources are not enough to meet the needs of the large number of displaced people. We appeal to humanitarian partners to provide more support.”

Ori said that only a collective response – involving regional government, host states, local authorities and NGOs – can properly respond to the crisis.

“Responsibility for displaced people is shared between the regional government, host states, local communities and humanitarian organisations,” he said.

“We coordinate efforts, seek relief assistance and monitor their conditions with local authorities. We bear part of the responsibility, but need greater cooperation to ease their suffering.”

Kheira Matar Hassan, a resident of Darfur, passed through Renk, Rabak and Khartoum at the start of the war before settling in al-Ghadir camp in 2023. She became separated from her husband when he went looking for work in a gold mining area in Chad at the same time.

She has received no word from him since he disappeared and has been left alone to support their seven children. They live in a dilapidated home built of bricks and mud bricks with damaged areas covered with cloth and plastic sheeting.

Hassan said she has received no support from the government or NGOs, and to support her children, she washes and irons clothes for families in the area, earning just enough money to buy food.

But her income is irregular, and if she has no customers, her family goes hungry. Lacking blankets or adequate shelter, she fears the impact that falling winter temperatures will have on her children. It stands in stark contrast to their former life, when her father worked as a farmer, and the family had enough food to eat.

“We are just here, trying to get by. Our circumstances are extremely difficult; we are really struggling here,” she told Al Jazeera.

“We came from an area where we were not poor. We had our land, cultivated it and lived off what it produced. But the war brought us here. Please look at us and consider our circumstances. We are really suffering.”

articles.title: A Massachusetts father invested his children's $56,600 college fund in cryptocurrency, cannabis and volatile stocks; an appeals court upheld an order requiring him to pay $55,868
articles.summary: A Massachusetts father who was allowed to invest his children’s college fund lost the protection of that flexibility after a court found he had failed to
articles.body: A Massachusetts father who was allowed to invest his children’s college fund lost the protection of that flexibility after a court found he had failed to preserve the money for their education. The account contained about $56,600.51 when the parents’ divorce agreement required him to preserve it for the children’s future educational expenses. The agreement also allowed him to invest and reinvest the funds as he chose. The father later claimed he had lost the money through investments in cryptocurrency, cannabis and other volatile stocks. The Massachusetts Appeals Court upheld a $55,868.02 order requiring him to pay towards his children’s college costs.The father was allowed to invest the college fund but had to preserve itThe case involved Heather Blaser and Kevin M. Blaser, who divorced in 2008 after having two children. According to the Massachusetts Appeals Court decision, their separation agreement included a provision titled “College Account for Children”. The account held approximately $56,600.51 and required the father to “preserve these funds” for the children’s future educational expenses.The same provision said he could invest and reinvest the money “in any manner he so chooses”. The Appeals Court found that this did not give him unlimited freedom to make reckless financial decisions. The court said the investment provision had to be read alongside the requirement to preserve the children’s college funds.In 2022, the mother brought a contempt complaint, alleging that the father had failed to preserve the money. A Probate and Family Court judge found him in contempt. The judge later ordered him to pay $55,868.02 towards the children’s post-secondary education costs, with half allocated to each child’s educational institution, according to the court record.Why the court rejected father’s explanation for where the money wentThe father argued that he had permissibly invested the college account funds and that his choices in cryptocurrency, cannabis and other volatile stocks had resulted in the loss of the money. The trial judge, though, found his testimony about the investments “not credible” and noted that he had failed to provide documentation supporting his account.The Appeals Court gave considerable deference to that credibility finding. It said the evidence supported the conclusion that the father had failed to preserve the funds, whether by spending them, moving them or otherwise withholding them from the children. The court therefore found no abuse of discretion in the contempt ruling.The father also challenged whether he had the ability to pay the $55,868.02 order. The trial judge had examined his income, expenses and liabilities and found problems with his financial disclosures, including undisclosed retirement savings and income or benefits from his father, who was also his employer.The Massachusetts Appeals Court upheld $55,868 order but sent part of case backThe Massachusetts Appeals Court, in a decision dated April 29, 2026, affirmed the contempt finding and upheld the order requiring the father to pay $55,868.02 towards the children’s college costs.The court did send the case back to the Probate and Family Court to clarify how the lump-sum payments should interact with the father’s separate obligation to pay one-third of the children’s college expenses. The judges said it was unclear whether the $55,868.02 would count towards that one-third obligation or be paid in addition to it.The Appeals Court also noted that if the combined payments exceeded the applicable 50% cap under the Massachusetts Child Support Guidelines, the lower court would need to make a specific finding that the father could afford to pay more than that limit. The contempt finding and $55,868.02 college-cost order otherwise remained in place, according to the court’s ruling.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Trump can’t get his calls returned’: Kim Jong Un ignores US President as North Korea expands nuclear arsenal capable of striking US cities
articles.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has not responded to US President Donald Trump's attempts to establish contact, while Pyongyang continues to expand its
articles.body: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has not responded to US President Donald Trump's attempts to establish contact, while Pyongyang continues to expand its nuclear arsenal and strengthen military ties with Russia, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal (WSJ).Trump attempted to reach Kim last year through established communication channels, including phone lines, but received no response. He subsequently wrote a letter to the North Korean leader, but US officials struggled to deliver it, the WSJ reported, citing people familiar with the matter.According to the report, White House officials devised an unusual plan to hand over the letter at North Korea's permanent mission to the United Nations in Manhattan. A group of officials waited outside the mission and handed the letter to a North Korean diplomat as he walked past. At a subsequent UN meeting, the diplomat reportedly placed the unopened letter in front of a US representative.The latest developments come as Trump's renewed efforts to meet Kim during his recent Asia trip failed to produce an agreement. The two sides explored the possibility of face-to-face talks in a last-minute diplomatic push, but Kim set conditions that Washington could not accept, people familiar with the discussions told the WSJ.During his first presidential term, Trump met Kim three times, with negotiations focused on denuclearising the Korean Peninsula. However, the North Korean leader has continued to expand his country's nuclear and missile capabilities since their last meeting in 2019.North Korea's nuclear arsenal expandsNorth Korea's nuclear capabilities have grown considerably since the breakdown of negotiations between Trump and Kim. According to the WSJ, the country's arsenal has increased from an estimated 20-30 nuclear warheads in 2019 to around 60.Pyongyang has also developed solid-fuel intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) capable of reaching the United States. Unlike liquid-fuel missiles, which require fuelling before launch and can be detected during preparations, solid-fuel systems can be stored ready for deployment and launched from mobile platforms, making them harder to track and intercept.The growing capabilities have raised concerns in Washington about the possibility that North Korea's nuclear status may be difficult to reverse. The US intelligence community's annual threat assessment last year acknowledged that "Kim has no intention of negotiating away his strategic weapons programs."In a February speech, Kim indicated that Washington could pursue peaceful coexistence by accepting North Korea's nuclear programme or face "eternal confrontation."Pyongyang is also seeking international recognition of its nuclear status, a position that could complicate future negotiations with the United States.Trump explored possible terms for renewed talksAccording to the WSJ, Trump's administration considered several proposals to create conditions for a meeting with Kim during the president's recent Asia trip.These included a possible formal end to the Korean War, which ended with an armistice more than seven decades ago, and a statement that would neither formally recognise North Korea as a nuclear weapons state nor explicitly demand the dismantling of its nuclear programme, a person familiar with the discussions told the newspaper.In exchange, Washington could seek limits on North Korea's nuclear and missile testing. Officials also considered establishing liaison offices as a possible first step towards more formal diplomatic relations.However, recognising North Korea as a nuclear weapons state would mark a major departure from longstanding US policy. Even entering negotiations without making denuclearisation a central demand could represent a shift in Washington's approach and raise concerns among allies, including South Korea and Japan, the WSJ reported, citing experts.A Trump administration official told the newspaper on Saturday that there had been no efforts to broker a meeting with Kim. North Korea's mission to the United Nations did not respond to requests for comment, the report said.The White House has maintained that it remains committed to North Korea's denuclearisation. However, people familiar with the matter told the WSJ that the administration lacks a detailed policy plan for dealing with Pyongyang.Unlike during Trump's first term, the administration has also left the special envoy position for North Korea policy vacant. The White House's national security strategy released last year did not mention North Korea, marking the first such omission since the end of the Cold War, according to the report.The Pentagon's National Defense Strategy, released in January, described North Korea as a "clear and present danger of nuclear attack on the American Homeland". However, unlike earlier versions, the document did not refer to North Korean denuclearisation.How Trump's earlier negotiations with Kim failedSuccessive US administrations have attempted to persuade North Korea to abandon its nuclear programme through diplomatic negotiations, economic incentives and sanctions.A 1994 agreement sought to freeze Pyongyang's plutonium production in exchange for economic assistance, sanctions relief and the construction of two light-water reactors. The arrangement collapsed in the early 2000s after Washington discovered that North Korea was pursuing a secret uranium-enrichment programme.The United States subsequently adopted the approach of Complete, Verifiable and Irreversible Dismantlement (CVID), demanding that North Korea give up its nuclear weapons programme.Trump initially adopted a hardline position during his first term, threatening tougher sanctions and warning of "fire and fury". In January 2017, after Kim announced preparations for the country's first intercontinental ballistic missile test capable of bringing the US within range, Trump wrote on social media, "It won’t happen!"North Korea went ahead with the test and conducted its sixth nuclear test later that year.After months of escalating rhetoric, Trump and Kim met in Singapore in June 2018, marking the first meeting between a sitting US president and a North Korean leader. The administration subsequently shifted from CVID to what it called Final, Fully Verified Denuclearization (FFVD).In a joint statement, Kim reaffirmed his commitment to work towards the complete denuclearisation of the Korean Peninsula. However, critics argued that the agreement lacked specific commitments and an enforceable roadmap.At their second summit in Hanoi in February 2019, Kim offered to shut down parts of the Yongbyon nuclear complex in exchange for the removal of UN sanctions restricting North Korea's trade. Washington, however, wanted Pyongyang to freeze its nuclear and missile programmes and agree to a roadmap for complete denuclearisation.The negotiations collapsed, with Trump leaving the summit without an agreement. North Korea subsequently resumed testing short-range ballistic missiles.The two leaders later exchanged letters and met again in the Korean Demilitarized Zone in June 2019. Despite the diplomatic engagement and high-profile photographs, the meeting failed to produce a lasting agreement.Russia and China strengthen North Korea's positionWith diplomatic efforts stalled, North Korea has expanded its military capabilities and developed closer ties with Russia.The relationship gained momentum after Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea backed Moscow and began supplying rockets and artillery ammunition, according to US officials cited by the WSJ.Kim met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Russia's Far East in September 2023, with Moscow promising assistance in areas including satellite development.By early 2024, officials in Ukraine, the United States and South Korea said North Korean short-range ballistic missiles were being used against Ukrainian targets.Russia also vetoed the renewal of the United Nations' monitoring mechanism for sanctions against North Korea in 2024, while China abstained from the vote.During Putin's visit to North Korea later that year, the two countries signed a mutual defence pact that revived Cold War-era commitments to provide assistance if either country came under attack. The agreement paved the way for North Korea to send troops to support Russia.The WSJ reported that North Korea's economy grew by 3.5% last year, marking its third consecutive year of growth above 3%. The report attributed the country's improved economic position partly to support from Russia and China.Pyongyang has also been accused of using cryptocurrency thefts to generate funds. According to the WSJ, North Korea was responsible for a cryptocurrency theft worth more than $6 billion from the Binance exchange, described in the report as the largest crypto heist in history. The United States later helped freeze nearly half of the stolen funds.Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis estimated that North Korea was responsible for 89% of cryptocurrency hacking losses worldwide this year, compared with 15% in 2021, the newspaper reported.China's approach towards North Korea has also appeared to shift. Beijing, which had previously opposed Pyongyang's nuclear ambitions, has increasingly called for a "fair and impartial" approach to peace on the Korean Peninsula rather than publicly demanding denuclearisation.Russian officials, meanwhile, have described North Korea's nuclear weapons as a reality that cannot be ignored.US faces questions over its North Korea policyThe growing nuclear threat has raised questions about Washington's ability to influence Pyongyang through diplomatic and economic pressure.Victor D. Cha, who served on former president George W. Bush's National Security Council and participated in multilateral negotiations with North Korea during the 2000s, told the WSJ that Washington was paying less attention to the issue.He has argued that arms control should replace denuclearisation as the starting point for future negotiations."For someone like me, it’s kind of like screaming in a forest," said Cha, who has posited that arms control should now supplant denuclearization as a starting point for talks. "Nobody is really paying attention."The challenge for the Trump administration is increasingly centred on dealing with a North Korea that has expanded its nuclear capabilities, strengthened international partnerships and shown little interest in returning to negotiations on Washington's earlier terms.You use AI every day. articles.title: The European revolt may be coming to the UK
articles.summary: There is enough justified anger among the British youth to spark a wave of mass protests.
articles.body:
The protests engulfing Europe represent a new level of popular mobilisation quite unlike any historical precedent. In France, Spain, Italy, Serbia, Germany and other countries across the continent, mass movements are challenging austerity and government failures.

On Friday, the United Kingdom saw what is likely to be the beginning of its own wave of youth-driven demonstrations. Thousands of students walked out of hundreds of schools and universities around the country, from Aberdeen to Brighton, Swansea to Nottingham, making it one of the largest student mobilisations since the tripling of tuition fees back in 2010.

The protests were called by organisations involved in the International Conference Against War, a pan-European initiative aimed at coordinating the movements against militarism. The University and College Union (UCU) was the first union to back the initiative with a National Day of Action, urging members across the university sector to hold protests and rallies alongside students.

That major unions followed UCU in supporting the walkouts, including Unison, Unite, the National Education Union (NEU), GMB and the Educational Institute of Scotland (EIS), speaks to the potential of union support.

In London, demonstrations from universities and colleges converged on Trafalgar Square to chants of “fight for our future, not their wars” before moving to Downing Street to hear student activists and trade union leaders berate the government for prioritising defence spending over education and public services.

There is indeed much for British youth to be angry about. Like in the rest of Europe, young people in the UK are facing a convergence of high inflation, unemployment, economic stagnation, the gutting of public services and deteriorating living standards, including a housing crisis stoked by property speculation. Combined with police brutality over solidarity with Palestine, unrestrained racism and sexism and expectations of environmental and climate catastrophe, mass protest is rather predictable.

According to government estimates, close to one million people between 16 and 24 years of age are “Neets” – not in education, employment or training; this is more than 13 percent of that age group. Young people make up more than 40 percent of the unemployed in the country. Apart from a tough job market, there is also a rampant mental health epidemic and an education system that few can afford.

Here we have the makings of a social and economic crisis waiting to happen, and yet the government response has been to seek more austerity.

It is a wonder that Alan Milburn, former Labour minister responsible for introducing private finance into the NHS in the late 1990s, was commissioned to write the controversial report on Neets for the government. Why bother to provide welfare when the private sector can solve the crisis? Unsurprisingly, Milburn’s recommendations are market-focused and include cutting certain benefits for youth, including for those with disabilities.

This comes on top of years of austerity in the higher education sector. Job cuts and course closures have become standard responses from university managements dealing with the lack of direct government funding. Many describe it as academic vandalism . What funding cuts have produced is extreme dysfunction, chaos and mismanagement: Faustian bargains with banks, management consultants and corporate outsourcing that serve efficiency and profit over quality provision.

While education and civilian job openings are dwindling, British youth are offered more opportunities in the army, which is now promoting a fully paid 18-month “foundation scheme”.

Military training, bolstered by a public campaign around “warfighting readiness” as part of last year’s Strategic Defence Review, was the brainchild of ministers under Keir Starmer, one of the most unpopular prime ministers in British history. True to form, Starmer pushed through an additional 15 billion pounds ($19.6bn) towards defence immediately before leaving office, for a total of 298 billion pounds ($389.8bn) over four years.

This is a worrying trend across Europe: While there are diminishing funds for public services, military spending is shooting up. This fact has not been lost on young people.

But what is driving this rearmament frenzy is that the European project is increasingly being bound together by NATO, along with Trump’s insistence that the EU should pay its fair share in maintaining the alliance. Support for Ukraine against Russia is at the centre of that project.

If youth mobilisation in the UK reaches the same level as in France, for example, this could be the first major test of Andy Burnham’s government. The French revolt was started over education – not the first strikes in French history over education, considering the origins of the 1968 uprisings. Still, France spends 5.1 percent of GDP on education .

The UK spends 4.1 percent of GDP on education, and even part of this budget has been diverted to defence, with less funding for schools in the coming years.

The UK has had seven prime ministers in the past decade, each one unable to deliver desperately needed income and wealth redistribution. A decade of Tory prime ministers allowed the rich to get very rich. Starmer continued the tradition. He was hammered by Reform and the Greens in the last local elections, firstly because he was unable to come through on the social democratic promises that many were hoping a Labour government would provide.

But second, he failed to recognise the genuine anger over British complicity in the Palestinian genocide, and then responded to mass protest with punitive legislation. Notwithstanding the Burnham bounce, the sitting prime minister has stuck to the same tack as his predecessor. His new foreign secretary has admitted that the government got it wrong over Palestine, but this needs to be backed up by action.

As Burnham faces growing protest, a heavy-handed approach will not work. Nor will more neoliberal reforms. A half-century of privatisation, deregulation and cuts to social welfare has produced the current malaise, and the crisis is only deepening.

The youth and the rest of European society are demanding change – real, lasting change in the political and economic spheres.

The revolutions that convulsed Europe in 1848 were a response to severe economic crisis, unemployment and bad harvests that caused famine. The European protests today unfold under comparable conditions. The task of those who want to see change is an internationalism that can generalise grievances, coordinate the movements and deliver concrete solidarity against austerity and war.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Dales Way Association locked out of own bank account for months
articles.summary: The Dales Way Association has been unable to access funds since September after a banking mix-up.
articles.body:
A walking charity has been left unable to access its own bank account for more than two months, describing the situation as an "absolute nightmare".

The Dales Way Association, which helps to protect and maintain an 80-mile footpath from Ilkley, in West Yorkshire, to Bowness, in Cumbria, has been unable to access funds after it tried to change the named signatory on its Virgin Money account.

Bev Downes, who was supposed to have taken over as charity treasurer, and her husband Ryk, who is the organisation's vice-chair, say they have been forced to pay £1,300 in charity wages and expenses out of their own pocket as a result.

Virgin Money has been contacted for comment.

"I can't close the account because it's not in my name," said Bev.

"I can't make any transactions. I can't pay anybody. I don't know what else to do, I'm lost.

"I've tried to call up and explain it to them and I was put through to the business team, who said, 'Sorry, we can't give you any information because your name is not on the account.'

"It's like we're in no-man's land, in limbo."

The couple said they had first tried to put Bev in charge of finances in May this year.

When attempts to complete the process in writing and over the phone did not work, Bev and Ryk went into Otley's banking hub to try to resolve the issue.

After filling out forms again with the assistance of Virgin Money staff at the start of September, they were still left unable to access the organisation's account.

Ryk and Bev said staff at the hub were similarly nonplussed as to why the process had not yet completed.

Meanwhile, the charity's former treasurer is also unable to access funds as his name was removed from the account.

Ryk, who is also a local Liberal Democrat councillor, added: "We've had members join the charity and set up a direct debit, but we can't see who's joined because we can't get any paperwork or statements.

"People have joined but we haven't been able to acknowledge their membership. We can't see what's coming in. It's absolute madness."

The Dales Way Association, which was set up in the 1960s, works with landowners to maintain walking access to the route as well as promoting accommodation providers along the path.

articles.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
articles.summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
articles.body:
Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.

His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.

Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.

The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".

The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.

Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.

The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.

"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media.

"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.

"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."

The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."

The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.

In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.

In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.

The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

articles.title: Harry Styles' rise to stardom from Holmes Chapel to headlining Glastonbury
articles.summary: The singer will make his debut at the festival next year as one of the event's curtain-raising artists.
articles.body:
When Harry Styles was just 16, his mother Anne secretly signed up him up for the ITV's The X Factor talent show in the hope of turning his singing dreams into a reality.

Fast forward more than 15 years later and the 32-year-old is set for a prestigious headline slot at Glastonbury 2027.

But how exactly did Styles' career rocket from his early years growing up in the Cheshire village of Holmes Chapel to leading one of the most coveted festival sets in the music industry?

Styles attended Hermitage Primary School in his village, which lies just 25 miles (40km) south of Manchester.

His year two teacher Helen Bailey fondly remembers how the seven-year-old "always had a cheeky little smile on his face".

"I just remember him always being really happy, really smiley, really popular with his friends," said Helen, who has worked at the school for 26 years.

Her colleague Kathryn Davies, who taught Styles in year three, also remembers his "cheeky personality".

"He was a real pleasure to teach, you know, across all areas of the curriculum," she said.

"He did have a sense of humour, but he knew when to stop. He had perfect timing, so he never pushed it too far."

The signs were there from an early age with Styles taking on a number of roles in the school's shows, including the lead role of Barney the mouse in a nativity and a conductor in Bugsy Malone.

"He had what we thought at the time was quite a small part," said Kathryn.

"He was the conductor of the orchestra, but he just knew how to hold the audience.

"He just used to turn around and give a little wink without any training at all.

"This role of conductor - that we thought was quite a small part because he'd have his bigger part in year six - became a bigger part than we anticipated."

Both Helen and Kathryn said they went on to watch with pride as his career blossomed.

"We're proud obviously of all the children, but I think we did see a star in the making when he was at school," said Helen.

"We're super proud but it's quite surreal."

For Kathryn, she hopes his career acts as an inspiration to the future generations who attend the school.

"It's nice to see that somebody who starts off here and can become so successful," she said.

"Hopefully the children who are here will see that for themselves and think 'well anybody can live out their dream'."

Styles went on to attend Holmes Chapel Comprehensive School.

"As Harry's ex head teacher I am so pleased that he has kept a place in his heart for his roots and for the village and school where he grew and thrived," said Nigel Bielby at the time.

The village has since become no stranger to so-called "Harries" - as his fans are often dubbed - who travel to Cheshire to explore the place where their idol grew up.

Among the popular destinations is W. Mandeville's bakery, where Styles worked part-time while at school.

In 2010, Styles travelled to his X Factor audition for his big break, earning a space in what would become the global phenomenon One Direction alongside Niall Horan, Liam Payne, Louis Tomlinson and Zayn Malik.

The boy band went on to release five albums in five years, dominating the music charts worldwide with their pop anthems.

With more than 200 million records sold worldwide, their music has received more than 21 billion streams across all platforms.

The band also won seven BRIT Awards, four MTV Music Awards, six Billboard Music Awards, seven American Music Awards and 28 Kids' Choice Awards.

Following the departure of Malik from the band in March 2015, the remaining members announced a break in order to pursue solo projects the following year.

Styles' debut solo single Sign of the Times was one of the most highly anticipated pop song of the year when it was released in 2017.

Since then he has released three albums in five years, with his fourth album Kiss All The Time, Disco Occasionally? put out earlier this year.

He has since received six Brit Awards, three Grammy Awards and two Ivor Novello Awards and enjoyed sold-out shows across the world.

Styles also turned his hand to acting with roles in Dunkirk, My Policeman and Don't Worry Darling.

And there's more. Styles was awarded a Guinness World Record for the longest run of concerts at Wembley Stadium after completing 12 sold-out shows for the London leg of his Together, Together tour in June.

The star has broken the official record for the longest residency by a musician at the venue in a single run, beating Coldplay's previous record of 10 nights in 2025.

His mother wrote at the time: "From this to this… What a weekend! Hard to get my heart in check.

"From stating back in 1996 that my little boy would end up on stage, doing what I had no idea, but his comedic timing, sunshine personality, and his beautiful soul was visible even then.

"How could I have possibly known then that he would break records doing exactly what he was put in this world to do, that he would grow up being the kind of man the world needs right now."

Now her "little boy" is set to headline Glastonbury - a monumental moment for all musicians and, of course, for Harry's millions of fans.

articles.title: Meet the twins turning small-town Evesham dreams into a feature film
articles.summary: Small Pond draws on the experiences of musicians and filmmakers who grew up in and around Evesham.
articles.body:
Twin brothers who once spent years chasing success in local bands are turning those experiences into a feature film shot in the streets, pubs and venues of their hometown.

Filming is nearly complete on Small Pond, an independent drama written and directed by Benji Parry and his twin brother Thom.

The pair have drawn heavily on Evesham and its music scene for a story about friendship, creativity and finding purpose when life does not quite go to plan.

The film follows two musicians from a small town who meet at a gig and forge an unlikely friendship. Although they come from different backgrounds, both are searching for somewhere they belong.

For Benji, the themes are deeply personal.

Growing up in Evesham, he spent his childhood making films with his parents' camcorder and persuading neighbours to appear in them.

Later came years performing in bands, experiences that helped shape the story now being brought to the screen.

He recalled making films as a child with friends and neighbours, joking that while school was not always a natural fit for him, filmmaking gave him a creative outlet.

"As a kid, I'd get my neighbours together and we'd make our own versions of films. Then I spent my 20s trying to make it in bands."

Throughout the years trying to making it with music though, Parry said the experiences would ultimately lead him towards filmmaking.

"I wouldn't say [the music] failed. It really grew me as who I am now and it allowed me to be a filmmaker," he says.

Elements of that journey can be seen in Small Pond, which explores holding on to creative ambitions, while living far from the bright lights and opportunities often associated with the arts.

Parry believes the experience will feel familiar to many people who grew up in smaller towns and have struggled to make it.

"I don't think it's really a thing where you're trying to make it as a filmmaker or be a rock star," he said.

Yet despite moving away for a period to look for success elsewhere, Parry found himself repeatedly returning to Evesham, both in life and in his writing.

"Whenever we write a script, it always just comes back to Evesham," he said. "You write what you know."

The production is embracing those roots at every opportunity.

Scenes are being filmed at recognisable locations including The Red Lion in Evesham and The Marrs Bar in Worcester, while local businesses have also been brought in to support the project.

But he does not see the film purely as a production.

"We're trying to form a community around this film," Parry said. "We're bringing in local businesses and putting a spotlight on them, because if all of us can gain something from this I think that's beautiful."

That collaborative spirit is one reason why actor Frankie Munchella, who grew up near Evesham, was keen to get involved.

"Everyone needs to really care for it to work," he said. "I'm just really invested in the project."

Co-star Stasi Cusack-Mercedez believes the film's appeal stretches well beyond Worcestershire.

Although many of its details are specific to Evesham, she says its story of searching for identity and pursuing a passion will resonate with audiences elsewhere.

"If they're from a small town anywhere in the world, maybe they'll connect with it," she said.

Music is central to the film. Alongside newly written material, the soundtrack draws on songs inspired by the Parry brothers' years in local bands, making the project what they describe as a love letter to the music scene that shaped them.

Support has also arrived from far beyond the Vale of Evesham.

A crowdfunding campaign has attracted backers from around the world, helping the filmmakers bring the project into production.

"It's such an uphill battle to make a movie," Parry said. "The fact people are believing in us that we've never met is overwhelming."

Filming is expected to continue this month, with the team hoping to complete the project by the end of the year before entering it into film festivals.

And while the brothers hope Small Pond will find audiences far and wide, they already know where they would like one of its most important screenings to take place.

Their ambition is to bring the finished film home, with a screening at Evesham's Regal Cinema.

articles.title: MP criticises Channel Island company ownership register plans
articles.summary: Sir Andrew Mitchell says access should be easier for people tackling financial crime.
articles.body:
Plans to improve transparency over company ownership in Guernsey and Jersey have come under criticism from a Westminster MP, who says they "do not go nearly far enough".

The comments come after Guernsey and Jersey set out plans to allow approved applicants access to information about who owns or controls companies when investigating suspected financial crime.

Sir Andrew Mitchell, who has campaigned for greater scrutiny of company ownership, said there were "immediate indications" the proposals would fall short.

He said limits on access to the information could mean "national security threats may remain entirely invisible to investigators".

The plans follow a joint commitment made by Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man in December 2023 to increase transparency around company ownership and help tackle money laundering, terrorist financing and other financial crime.

Currently, information about who ultimately owns or controls companies is generally only available to law enforcement agencies, regulators and certain regulated businesses carrying out anti-money laundering checks.

The new proposals would allow journalists, academics and other applicants with a legitimate interest to apply for access.

Sir Andrew said investigators could face a "catch-22" because they may need access to the register to prove wrongdoing in the first place.

He also said he understood applicants would have to show they had been unable to find the information elsewhere, arguing: "This entirely defeats the object of a register."

Jersey's consultation response says applicants would be expected to show that "all reasonable alternative sources have been exhausted" before access was granted.

Guernsey's published response does not explicitly set out the same requirement.

He said: "Access should be open to those from other jurisdictions, for example those in the global south from whom much of the world's dirty money was stolen in the first place."

Sir Andrew also questioned whether users would have to pay to access the information, saying: "This information should be free at the point of access."

He said the proposals should eventually lead to fully public registers.

Both the governments of Guernsey and Jersey rejected Sir Andrew's criticism and said they continue to meet international standards in tackling financial crime.

A Government of Jersey spokesperson said the concerns raised by him "do not accurately reflect what is in Jersey's consultation response paper".

They said the policy was intended to help Jersey meet its international commitments while maintaining "a fair, proportionate, and effective transparency framework".

They added: "Jersey continues to meet international standards for transparency and countering money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing."

Deputy Andrew Niles, from Guernsey's Policy & Resources Committee, rejected Sir Andrew's criticism and pointed to a positive 2025 assessment of the island's efforts to tackle financial crime .

He said: "Guernsey does not accept the suggestion that our proposals fall short of the commitments we've made on beneficial ownership transparency or that the island does not meet international standards on beneficial ownership transparency."

He said the framework would provide access for people with a legitimate interest in investigating crime while protecting privacy and vulnerable individuals.

"The proposal is based on a tried and tested model adopted in the EU," he added.

articles.title: Welsh Midwives told to expect fewer jobs as 2027 recruitment drive is paused
articles.summary: One graduate said she would take minimum wage to get her first job in widwifery.
articles.body:
Midwives who will graduate in Wales next year have been told there are fewer jobs available for them than expected.

The Royal College of Midwives said this is in addition to the 66 newly qualified midwives who didn't manage to find a job after they graduated last year.

Director of RCM Cymru Julie Richards said the situation was "unacceptable" when maternity services are "facing pressure from every direction" .

The Welsh government said it recognised the concerns around employment uncertainty and it was working with NHS Wales "to understand workforce pressures and requirements".

Kimmy Williams, 37, from Swansea has had to return to her old job working in the kitchen at a local college because there aren't enough midwifery graduate jobs available in Wales.

Williams said she's aware that almost half of her peers on the midwifery course at Swansea University are yet to find a job despite the promise of employment for everyone once they graduated.

Her dream job was to become a midwife after having children of her own 16 years ago, but she has instead been left with "a mountain of debt and no job at the end of it".

"Now I'm just working in the same job I was previously but worse off financially," she added.

Williams said she would accept minimum wage to do the job initially just to be able to get into the system and progress her career.

The Royal College of Midwives said students across Wales are facing the same "deepening crisis".

Megan Lewis, from Cardiff, said it's hard to understand why so many newly qualified midwives in Wales, like her, are not able to get a job after witnessing first hand how "stretched" services can become.

"Midwives regularly told us how much they valued having students on shift because we were another pair of hands to help with care," she said.

Midwifery students have their tuition fees paid by NHS Wales on the condition they commit to working in the country for up to two years after they graduate.

Although a number of jobs may come up at some health boards, RCM Cymru said it had not been confirmed how many vacancies will become available, but they were "challenging the suggestion that improved retention is behind the lack of jobs for newly qualified midwives in Wales".

Richards said RCM Cymru's members had told them they were working "under enormous pressure".

"They are working above their contracted hours, they're missing breaks, many are having their training cancelled," she added.

"Quite clearly there is a need for these graduate midwives to enter into the workforce now."

Health Education and Improvement Wales (HEIW) said the NHS would not be running a national recruitment round in spring 2027 as "very few roles" are expected to become available.

HEIW said midwife turnover in NHS Wales is at its lowest level for over 16 years meaning "fewer roles have become available than expected".

It also said financial pressures have limited the number of Band 5 roles health boards can offer to newly qualified midwives.

Chief executive Alex Howells said HEIW was "working with health boards to establish what roles they can offer and how graduates can apply."

articles.title: Indonesia factory fire kills three, 36 missing
articles.summary: At least 15 people rescued, including 4 taken to hospital, as authorities say cause of the fire is under investigation.
articles.body:
A fire at a sweets factory in Indonesia has killed at least three people and 36 others are missing.

Photos and videos circulating online on Sunday showed flames and thick smoke coming from the Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Banten province, which borders the capital Jakarta. Footage from inside the three-storey building appeared to show the fire caused extensive damage, with equipment blackened and destroyed.

A company representative said 300 workers were inside when the blaze started. He added that 54 were initially missing, but 15 have since been rescued. Four of them were taken to hospital, said the National Search and Rescue Agency in a statement.

“The fire is still burning in several locations and firefighting teams are continuing extinguishing and cooling operations,” rescue official Rizky Dwianto told The Associated Press news agency.

Firefighters from Serang district and Banten province were battling flames in several parts of the facility more than 12 hours after the fire began, Dwianto said.

Rescue workers along with fire department personnel and the Indonesian Red Cross searched different sections of the factory, focusing on areas where victims might be trapped, he added.

The disaster agency said the cause of the fire was under investigation.

Local broadcasters and social media accounts shared footage of families gathering outside the factory.

The factory produces milk-based snacks and sweets, known as Milkita.

Indonesia has suffered a number of deadly fires in recent years. A fire in an office building in Jakarta killed at least 22 people last December. An explosion at an Indonesian nickel-processing plant killed at least 13 people in 2023.

articles.title: Gwalior family finds iron blade inside Dettol soap after child suffers cheek cut; consumer commission orders Reckitt India to pay Rs 50,000, shopkeeper and distributor Rs 2,000 each
articles.summary: BHOPAL: A complaint over a blade found inside a Dettol soap bar has resulted in a Rs 54,000 compensation order against the manufacturer, distributor and
articles.body: BHOPAL: A complaint over a blade found inside a Dettol soap bar has resulted in a Rs 54,000 compensation order against the manufacturer, distributor and retailer, after a Gwalior consumer commission held that inadequate quality checks had exposed a child to a potential health hazard.The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Gwalior, passed the order on November 17, partly allowing a complaint filed by Angad Singh Tomar against Mohit Kirana Store, the soap distributor and Reckitt (India) Ltd, the manufacturer of Dettol soap.According to the complaint, Tomar purchased a Dettol soap bar from Mohit Kirana Store on May 21, 2025. While his minor son was using it during a bath, a sharp cut appeared on the child’s cheek. On examining the soap, the family found an iron blade embedded inside it.Tomar approached the shopkeeper with the complaint, following which the retailer replaced the soap bar. However, the family was shocked to find another blade inside the replacement bar as well.The complainant subsequently lodged a complaint with the National Consumer Helpline on May 27, 2025, alleging that the matter had not been satisfactorily resolved. He later approached the consumer commission on June 17, 2025, seeking Rs 3.5 lakh as compensation for physical and mental harassment, besides Rs 50,000 towards litigation expenses.The retailer argued that he was merely selling the soap and had purchased it from the distributor. The manufacturer, meanwhile, maintained that stringent quality-control procedures were followed during production, including the use of two metal detectors to identify and remove foreign metal particles.The company also claimed that it had purchased 21 soap bars from the same batch through the retailer and subjected 14 of them to testing at an FDA-recognised laboratory, where no defect was detected. It suggested that the blade could have been deliberately inserted into the soap.However, the commission observed that the manufacturer had failed to produce evidence establishing that the particular soap bar supplied to the complainant had undergone the claimed quality checks. It also noted that there was no proof of inspection after the soap was frozen, packed and made ready for sale.The panel observed that merely testing other soap bars from the same batch did not establish that the defective bar was free of foreign material. It also rejected the manufacturer’s suggestion that the complainant might have deliberately inserted the blade, observing that no credible evidence had been produced to support the allegation.In its final order dated November 17, 2026, the commission directed Reckitt (India) Ltd to pay Rs 50,000 compensation to the complainant within 45 days. The retailer and distributor were each directed to pay Rs 2,000. The manufacturer was also ordered to pay Rs 2,000 towards litigation expenses. A 6% annual interest will apply to the compensation amounts if payment is delayed beyond the stipulated period.The complaint was thus partly allowed, with the commission holding the manufacturer liable for deficiency in service and the retailer and distributor responsible for their respective lapses.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhopal | Silver Rate in Bhopal | Bank Holidays in Bhopal | Public Holidays in Bhopal | Petrol Price in Bhopal | Diesel Price in Bhopal | CNG Price in Bhopal | LPG Price in BhopalStay updated with the latest Bhopal news. articles.title: 'No place for hate in cricket’: Congress leader rejects Masood’s religious bias charge over Siraj
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Mumtaz Patel has rejected party colleague Imran Masood's allegation of religious discrimination in the selection of the Indian
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Mumtaz Patel has rejected party colleague Imran Masood's allegation of religious discrimination in the selection of the Indian cricket team, saying players have always been picked on the basis of form and suitability rather than religion, caste or region.Patel's remarks came after Masood alleged that fast bowler Mohammed Siraj was left out of India's playing eleven for the first Test against New Zealand because of his religious identity. Speaking to news agency ANI, Patel said cricket should remain separate from the communal divisions seen in political discourse."In cricket as a sport, I think there is no space for hate or this religious divide. Firstly, when we talk about Team India, I think the most prominent thing in that is India, and we've always seen cricket in its highest form. I would say that this religious divide, hate divide, is not acceptable," she said.Patel maintained that team selections were based on players' performances and the requirements of a particular tournament."I think cricketers with the best form, best suited in that particular tournament as a team, have always been put together. I doubt I have never seen cricket being divided in the name of states, religion, culture, caste or anything. Let's keep this away," she said.She also criticised political messaging that, in her view, contributed to an atmosphere of division, referring to campaign slogans and remarks by leaders without naming them."At the same time I want to say that let's not create this atmosphere of hate and divide in our country. When you have top leaders on stage talking about people being identified by their clothes, or leaders saying 'batenge toh katenge', it creates a negative atmosphere in the country. Let's keep all this separate. Let's be a united India and especially when it comes to cricket, we are united as Team India," Patel added.Earlier on Saturday, Congress Rajya Sabha MP Ranjeet Ranjan had also urged Masood to keep politics and sports separate, saying athletes should not be drawn into political discourse."...I would simply urge Masood-ji to keep politics and sports separate; please, let us not interfere in sports. Sports has its own domain, its own criteria for merit, and every player has their own unique struggle. I strongly believe that while we may engage in political manoeuvring, we should not drag sports or athletes into our political discourse. I find that completely unacceptable..," Ranjan said.The controversy began on Friday after Masood questioned Siraj's omission from the playing eleven, alleging that the decision was linked to his name and religion."It is being said that despite his good performance, he was not given a place in the team. His name is 'Siraj', and that is why he was not given a place. If you are not selecting him despite his good performance, the discrimination is clear," Masood told ANI.On Saturday, Masood cited fast bowler Mohammed Shami and batter Sarfaraz Khan while questioning the selection process."There's Mohammed Shami, there's Sarfaraz, and many others. Selections should be based on performance; if someone is performing well, it shouldn't matter where they come from," he said.Questions over Siraj's omission have also drawn attention to his record in the ongoing World Test Championship cycle. He has taken 43 wickets in 11 matches, according to the information cited in the reports.India selected Jasprit Bumrah, Prasidh Krishna, Akash Deep and Anshul Kamboj as its four pacers for the Test, alongside Washington Sundar. The team management cited its bowling combination and the need for additional batting cover.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
