articles.title: Watch: Hours after PM Modi inaugurates Nitish Setu, RJD workers tear down NDA banners
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A political showdown erupted on Bihar’s newly inaugurated Nitish Setu on Saturday, with Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) workers pulling down banners
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A political showdown erupted on Bihar’s newly inaugurated Nitish Setu on Saturday, with Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) workers pulling down banners and posters put up by the ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA), hours after Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the bridge in Vaishali.Videos circulating on social media showed a large group of RJD supporters, tearing down the displays and shouting slogans in support of party supremo Lalu Prasad Yadav and leader of opposition Tejashwi Yadav. Police personnel were seen moving alongside the crowd but appeared unable to control the gathering.The disruption has triggered a fresh exchange between the BJP and RJD, turning the inauguration of a major infrastructure project into a political flashpoint.BJP has accused the RJD of trying to politicise a development project rather than acknowledge its benefits. The bridge, named Nitish Setu, was inaugurated by PM Modi on November 21. The six-lane structure has been built at an estimated cost of Rs 4,280 crore and connects Kacchi Dargah with Bidupur. It is expected to improve connectivity between north and south Bihar and reduce pressure on Mahatma Gandhi Setu.Row over the bridge’s nameThe naming of a bridge in Bihar has triggered a political row, with the Congress and RJD questioning the decision to christen it Nitish Setu instead of naming it after Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru.Congress leader Pawan Khera accused the BJP-led Bihar government of hurting Sikh sentiments through the decision. In a post on X, he questioned why a bridge proposed to be named after Guru Gobind Singh was now being named after Nitish Kumar, and whether the move was aimed at pushing the former chief minister out of the political mainstream. "Why is this being done in a way that tramples on the sentiments of the Sikh community?" he asked.Khera also questioned the timing, saying it raised concerns about whether the JD(U) leader was being sidelined while still alive. He shared a Bihar Road Construction Department document containing a note on a non-official resolution moved by RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav regarding the proposed name.Tejashwi had earlier said he moved a private member's resolution in the Bihar Assembly proposing the bridge be named after Guru Gobind Singh. He accused the government of changing its position and said the decision was politically motivated. The Bihar Assembly later said no decision had been taken in the House to name the bridge after Guru Gobind Singh.The controversy has also drawn criticism from AAP leaders in Punjab. Finance minister Harpal Singh Cheema, Assembly speaker Kultar Singh Sandhwan and MLA Kuldeep Singh Dhaliwal urged the Bihar government to reconsider, saying the bridge's proximity to Takht Sri Patna Sahib made the issue particularly sensitive. Cheema said the government could honour Nitish Kumar in other ways, but going back on a proposal to honour Guru Gobind Singh was unacceptable. Dhaliwal called the decision an insult to Sikh sentiments.Tejashwi also questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi's inauguration of the bridge, claiming Nitish Kumar had opened it around 17 months earlier and that the project was already in use. He challenged the BJP to identify its contribution to the construction.The inauguration also brought back a familiar election-season image: PM Modi waved his gamcha during the event, recalling his appearance at the BJP office in Patna after the NDA’s victory in the 2025 Bihar assembly elections. The gesture had gone viral at the time, with “Modi Ka Gamcha” trending online after the alliance won 202 of the state’s 243 seats.The bridge inauguration was attended by Bihar governor Lt Gen Syed Ata Hasnain (retd), Union minister Chirag Paswan, chief minister Samrat Choudhary and other dignitaries.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A London neighbour withdrew permission to use a passageway leading to a shared garden; a dispute involving a forced gate, changed locks and washing on her patio ended with a £20,000 legal-cost order
articles.summary: A disagreement over who could walk through a narrow passageway at a London property developed into a legal dispute involving damaged locks, a forced gate
articles.body: A disagreement over who could walk through a narrow passageway at a London property developed into a legal dispute involving damaged locks, a forced gate and privacy complaints. At the centre of the case was Jodie Schloss, a resident who had allowed other occupants of her building to reach a shared garden through a passage beside her flat for years. She eventually withdrew that permission, saying she no longer wanted people passing so close to her home. But Robin Larkins and his elderly father, Derek, challenged the decision, arguing that other residents should not lose access to the garden. As reported by The Independent, the dispute reached court, where the pair were ordered to pay £20,000 towards their neighbour's legal costs.London neighbour dispute begins after shared garden access is withdrawnThe dispute concerned a Victorian villa in Strathray Gardens, Swiss Cottage, north London, where Schloss and Robin Larkins both occupy garden flats. The property also contains several other flats, with some reportedly selling for more than £2 million.For approximately three decades, residents living elsewhere in the building had been able to reach the rear garden through a passage running alongside Schloss's home. She had previously provided keys allowing them to use the route.That arrangement changed in August 2025. Schloss decided she no longer wanted people walking past her front door and withdrew the permission she had previously given. Her legal representative later told the court that the decision was motivated by concerns about privacy, particularly because the passage runs immediately beside her entrance.The change created a disagreement over the practical use of the garden. Although Robin Larkins could reach it directly from his own flat through a back door, the other occupants did not have an equivalent route, according to the evidence presented at the hearing.CCTV footage features in row over damaged passageway gateThe situation became more contentious in September 2025, when the arguments over access developed into allegations of trespass and interference with the gate. Schloss's barrister, John Clargo, told the court that Derek Larkins had insisted he was entitled to continue using the passage on 1 September. His son allegedly threatened to remove the gate. Schloss later heard two men discussing whether she was away from the property, and the following morning she discovered damage to the lock.She subsequently found further damage when she returned to collect belongings on 6 September. CCTV footage also became part of the dispute, with Schloss alleging that it showed Robin Larkins had been involved in damaging the lock. The police were contacted after she was informed that Robin, Derek and another person were in the passageway. According to the account given in court, she initially agreed to provide Robin with a key but reconsidered after viewing footage that appeared to show his father using a crowbar.The disagreement did not end there. On 2 October, Robin Larkins changed the gate's lock without providing Schloss with a key, despite a request from her solicitor. She subsequently changed the locks again.Family laundry found on neighbour's private patio amid garden access rowThe passageway remained a point of contention into the following year. Schloss's legal team told the court that Derek Larkins forced the lock on 22 March 2026, allowing the pair to use the route on that date and again on 24 March. A separate incident on 9 April brought another complaint. Washing belonging to the Larkins family was found hanging out to dry on Schloss's private patio.Robin Larkins addressed the matter during the hearing, saying his cleaner had put the laundry there without realising that the space was private. He added that the cleaner had been instructed not to repeat the mistake. For Schloss, the incidents formed part of a wider pattern of unwanted access to areas she considered her own. She approached the court seeking an injunction to prevent further entry onto the passageway and patio.Her barrister argued that the other occupants had no legal entitlement to use the route simply because they had done so for many years. He also maintained that Robin's right to use the garden did not give him permission to cross his neighbour's passageway.Robin Larkins said he wanted to protect other residents' accessRepresenting himself, Robin Larkins disputed the suggestion that his actions were malicious. He told the court that his concern was primarily about the other leaseholders in the building, who had relied on the side passage to reach the garden for around 30 years.He argued that residents had contributed towards garden maintenance through their service charges and should not suddenly be prevented from using the communal space. Larkins said the dispute did not directly affect his own access because he could enter the garden from his flat. His objection, he explained, was about the position of the other occupants, who had no alternative route.Derek Larkins also had a long-standing connection with the property. He had worked as its gardener and general maintenance man for years, a role that involved accessing manholes in the passageway and moving between the garden and other parts of the building.Judge Stephen Hellman, sitting at Mayor's and City County Court, acknowledged that the withdrawal of access would have come as a surprise to the other residents. He also recognised that the passage was the only way most of them could reach the garden.However, the judge considered the circumstances surrounding the damaged gate and the repeated use of the passage when assessing the conduct of the defendants.Judge orders father and son to pay £20,000 in legal costsAfter a hearing lasting around three hours, Judge Hellman accepted legally binding undertakings from Robin and Derek Larkins. Both agreed not to enter Schloss's passageway or private patio without her permission while the wider dispute remained unresolved.The judge also ordered the father and son to pay £20,000 towards Schloss's legal costs. A significant factor in that decision was the conduct surrounding the gate, which the judge heard had been forced open twice by Derek, with his son present on one occasion.The order followed an interim hearing rather than a final determination of every issue between the neighbours. The court is expected to consider the wider dispute at a full trial at a later date, unless the parties reach an agreement beforehand. Judge Hellman indicated that Schloss had a strong case concerning the passageway and warned the defendants that continuing the proceedings unsuccessfully could leave them facing considerably higher legal expenses.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available online reports. The Times of India has not independently verified the details of the neighbour dispute or the court proceedings. The £20,000 order relates to legal costs, and the wider dispute remains subject to further court proceedings.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Estonia to close border with Russia, Moscow decries ‘new Iron Curtain’
articles.summary: VILNIUS — Estonia will close its road border crossings with Russia on security grounds for at least six months, the Baltic country’s government said on Friday, prompting a warning from Moscow that it ​would respond with political and diplomatic measures.
articles.body: VILNIUS — Estonia will close its road border crossings with Russia on security grounds for at least six months, the Baltic country’s government said on Friday, prompting a warning from Moscow that it ​would respond with political and diplomatic measures. NATO and E.U. member Estonia on Sunday accused Russian security services ​of staging an attempted arson attack on an Estonian defense company, in what ⁠it said was the second such incident this year. The border closure is set to begin ​on December 1. This would help address the wider security situation and limit Russia’s ability to organise further attacks, ​Estonian Interior Minister Igor Taro told a press conference. “Russian security services are intimidating and trying to recruit our citizens who are travelling through our border checkpoints. This is something we cannot tolerate anymore,” Taro said. The Kremlin has denied any ​involvement in the weekend arson attack. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Friday said that Russia would ​respond with political and diplomatic measures if Estonia went ahead with the closure. “Such moves are tantamount to attempts to ‌erect ⁠a new Iron Curtain under the false pretence of some sort of threat from the East,” Zakharova said. Estonia, a strong supporter of Ukraine, currently has five crossing points where travellers can enter or leave Russia, according to the government. Estonia’s northern neighbour Finland shut its Russia border crossings in 2023, and has ​kept them closed since ​then, while southern Baltic ⁠nations Latvia and Lithuania maintain open crossings. Thousands of people living in Estonia have family in Russia or vice versa, as legacies of the Soviet era. ​The crossing at Narva, a majority Russian-speaking city on the Estonian side ​of the ⁠border, is also used by people travelling from further afield in Europe to reach St Petersburg a few hours’ drive away. Of the 760,000 people who crossed the Estonia-Russia border this year, 307,000 were Russian nationals, ⁠175,000 were ​Estonian citizens and 54,000 held Finnish passports, Estonian police ​data showed. Rail freight is not affected by the road closure, but remains subject to strict customs checks, Estonia said.

articles.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
articles.summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.
articles.body:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.

He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.

The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.

"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.

"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.

The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.

Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.

These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.

His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.

This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.

This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.

The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.

It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.

Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.

All this made even honest test takers paranoid.

Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.

Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

articles.title: In 2022, a New York family partnership bought Galloo Island for $5.8 million; a $3 million conservation easement now protects 1,410 acres on Lake Ontario without transferring ownership or opening the island to visitors
articles.summary: A privately owned island in Lake Ontario has received permanent conservation protection after a major agreement with a New York land trust.
articles.body: A privately owned island in Lake Ontario has received permanent conservation protection after a major agreement with a New York land trust. The Thousand Islands Land Trust (TILT) has secured a conservation easement covering 1,410 acres of Galloo Island, protecting its forests, wetlands, shoreline and wildlife habitats from future development. The agreement, reported by local broadcaster WWNY and The Land Report, is the largest conservation project by acreage in TILT’s history. The organisation announced the protection as a significant step towards safeguarding one of the region’s ecologically important landscapes.A $3 million deal to protect the islandThe conservation agreement was completed in partnership with Galloo Island Farms, the family partnership that acquired the property in December 2021 for $5.8 million. The purchase was made by the Patten family, which had previously owned much of the island and returned with plans to restore its farmland and protect its natural landscape.According to The Land Report, the conservation easement is valued at approximately $3.1 million, while WWNY reported the expenditure at $3 million. It is the largest single conservation expenditure made by the Thousand Islands Land Trust. The easement covers roughly 70 per cent of Galloo Island, making it a substantial addition to the region’s protected land. The agreement was negotiated between TILT, Galloo Island Farms and the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation.Ownership remains with the Patten familyDespite the conservation agreement, Galloo Island has not become public property. The Patten family retains ownership of the protected land, and the easement does not amount to a sale or transfer of the island to the land trust. Instead, it is a legally binding arrangement that places restrictions on how the property can be used and developed. These conditions are intended to ensure that the island’s natural features remain protected even if ownership changes in the future.The agreement also does not make Galloo Island a new tourist destination. Visitors cannot assume they have public access to the property, and restrictions extend to activities around the shoreline, including fishing. The arrangement is an example of how conservation easements allow private landowners to retain their property while permanently limiting activities that could damage its environmental value.Why Galloo Island matters to conservationistsLocated in Lake Ontario, Galloo Island is recognised for its diverse natural habitats, including forests, wetlands, grasslands and extensive shoreline. These environments provide shelter and feeding grounds for a range of wildlife, including rare, threatened and endangered species.The island also serves as an important stopover for migratory birds and monarch butterflies. Among the wildlife recorded in the area are short-eared owls and golden eagles. For TILT, protecting the island is particularly significant because of its ecological importance and the development pressures it has faced over the years. Earlier proposals for wind energy projects had raised concerns about the island’s future, although neither project ultimately moved forward. The latest conservation agreement provides long-term protection for the landscape while allowing the property to remain privately owned.A significant addition to New York’s conservation effortsFounded in 1984, the Thousand Islands Land Trust works to protect natural landscapes, wildlife habitats, water quality and outdoor recreation opportunities across the Thousand Islands region, which stretches along the US-Canada border. According to its website, the organisation has protected more than 15,000 acres through land ownership and conservation easements. Its portfolio includes forests, wetlands, shoreline properties and nature preserves.The Galloo Island agreement adds to those efforts and marks TILT’s first conservation easement purchase in the eastern part of Lake Ontario. While the island will remain privately owned and unavailable for general public recreation, its forests, wetlands and wildlife habitats now have an additional layer of permanent legal protection. The agreement ensures that the island’s ecological value will be considered in how the land is managed for generations to come.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Photos: People rally across France over living costs, public services
articles.summary: Protests held on sixth weekend as tens of thousands march over inequality and organisers plan more rallies.
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of people have marched in cities across France for the sixth consecutive weekend to demand better public services and express anger over the rising cost of living and deepening inequality.

The protest movement, sparked in mid-September by high school students calling for improved learning conditions, has since fuelled a nationwide campaign against soaring prices, failing public services and police brutality.

Across the country, organisers reported 150,000 protesters on Saturday, down from 200,000 last week and 800,000 during the first of the weekly demonstrations on October 17.

The Ministry of the Interior said numbers have “significantly declined” as it put Saturday’s turnout at 82,500 people, compared with 106,000 a week earlier.

The protests have been largely peaceful but have seen sporadic violence on the margins and repeated accusations of police brutality.

Last month, huge rallies across France descended into the worst rioting seen in years with hundreds of shops looted and buildings attacked and set on fire.

Unions and activists have called for further protests in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Restored wells bring life back to Hebron’s occupied Old City
articles.summary: Hebron’s Old City has been under constant siege by Israeli settlers and the military.
articles.body:
Hebron, Occupied West Bank – Water shortages have created a constant hardship that threaten the Palestinian identity of the historic area of occupied Hebron’s Old City. For Umm Mohammad Jaber, who lives with her family of four, the lack of water makes simple household tasks – from preparing meals to cleaning – a daily challenge.

“People may be able to endure going without food or electricity, but without water, life comes to a standstill,” the 48-year-old told Al Jazeera.

The narrow streets of Hebron’s Old City and the plethora of checkpoints and military gates that encircle it mean that water tankers struggle to reach Palestinian homes.

Municipal water, meanwhile, reaches Umm Mohammed’s home only once a month and the family lacks the storage capacity to keep enough supplies until the next source arrives.

Settlers who occupy the rooftops of Palestinian homes and shops in the Old City make it difficult for locals to install water tanks, which might be one way to solve the water crisis. Instead, Palestinians are now turning to a traditional but forgotten water source lying beneath their feet.

After monitoring water shortages over the past two years, the Hebron Rehabilitation Committee launched a project to restore the abandoned wells of Hebron’s Old City.

Muhannad al-Jaabari, director general of the committee, said residents of the Old City were invited to register neglected wells in their properties when the project launched in July last year with the aim of restoring them and providing families with a reliable source of clean water.

More than 70 households did so in the first few days of the campaign and around 215 have registered since. The committee has so far restored 108 wells and aims to complete work on the remainder next year.

Al-Jaabari said the project serves three interconnected goals: preserving the wells as part of the Old City’s heritage and architectural fabric, improving access to water supplies, and strengthening residents’ ability to remain in their homes and neighbourhoods amid immense pressure from Israeli settlers and authorities to leave. “Finding water means bringing life to the Old City,” he said.

The committee has restored around 40 wells in closed areas, parts of the city where Israel maintains strict military control, in cooperation with the International Committee of the Red Cross, where water tankers faced difficulties reaching residents due to restrictions on movement.

Hebron’s Old City has been under Israeli occupation since 1967 and remains under Israeli military control but should be under Palestinian civil jurisdiction. Hebron has been subject to relentless assaults by Israeli settlers since the 1980s, who have occupied parts of the Old City and suffocated life there for Palestinian residents.

Al-Jaabari said the work of the committee is to make ordinary life possible for Palestinians so they can remain in the area and that a critical way of doing this is ensuring households have access to water.

Restoring the wells allows water to be stored and used by households when needed. It also helps essential institutions, such as schools, to continue to provide vital services to Palestinian families in the Old City.

Al-Jazaer Basic Boys’ School, which has 136 students, has faced persistent water shortages for almost two years due to the expansion of settler outposts in the Old City. It has made bringing water into Palestinian homes and buildings a huge challenge.

Principal Hisham al-Qawasmeh said the school relied on water tanks and frequently had to request additional supplies, so it turned to the committee for help.

Following the restoration of a well inside the school, students, teachers and staff now have a steady supply of water for drinking, cleaning and other daily needs.

Al-Qawasmeh estimates the well’s capacity at between 400 and 500 cubic metres, which is expected to reduce the school’s dependence on external deliveries. He stresses that maintaining essential services is closely linked to the continuation of education and the ability of families to remain in the Old City.

“If there is no water and no school, these 70 families will naturally look for an alternative and that alternative will be outside the Old City.”

He adds that restoring the school building and its well helps support students and their families and sustain the neighbourhood. “We were suffering from water shortages, so we restored the well to address this problem, which had persisted for years,” al-Qawasmeh said. “Schools consume more water than homes and water is the lifeblood of every place.”

Behind the reopening of the wells lies demanding technical work, requiring considerable effort and caution. Deep wells and areas under movement restrictions present particular challenges, said Khaled al-Sharif, a supervisor for the Old City well restoration project. The process varies for each well but inevitably includes pumping out leftover water, removing dirt and rubble, replastering well walls, waterproofing, disinfecting and refilling them with fresh water.

With water, electricity and pumping equipment at play, the work is not without its dangers for the teams. With huge amounts of rubble needing to be excavated and materials for restoration brought into the closed areas, it is also not without its challenges.

“Hebron is suffering from a severe water shortage. And when we talk about the Old City, we are talking about the difficulty of water tankers entering it because of its narrow alleyways,” al-Sharif said.

He describes the restoration project as a practical response to an essential need, one that directly improves residents’ living conditions and helps them remain in the area amid the pressure of displacement.

Restoring wells is part of a wider effort by the committee to preserve the Palestinian presence and identity of the Old City. The number of Jewish settlement outposts in the Old City has increased from four before the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023 to 12 today, according to the committee. This expansion appears intended to push Palestinian families, many having owned property in the Old City for generations, out of the area and replace them with a Jewish Israeli settler contingent.

To counter this, the committee has launched a number of projects aimed at improving living standards for Palestinian families in the Old City and has rehoused more than 54 families in homes across the Old City since October 7, while dozens of other families are waiting for suitable housing.

The return of families to their restored homes has helped thwart displacement plans and reaffirm Palestinians’ attachment to their land, the Old City and the Ibrahimi Mosque, which has also repeatedly been besieged by Israeli settlers.

Daoud Hassan, 33, who has three children and is from Hebron, worked in construction in Israel. But following a ban on the entry of Palestinian workers after the start of the genocidal war on Gaza, he has been unable to find work and struggled to pay rent.

With the help of the committee, Hassan moved into a renovated abandoned home in the Old City seven months ago through the initiative, free of charge, helping not just his family continue to survive but also maintain the Palestinian identity of Hebron.

“We moved to the Old City because of our economic circumstances and to preserve our history and heritage,” he said.

articles.title: Fire at Indonesian candy factory leaves 3 dead and dozens of workers unaccounted for
articles.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia — A fire swept through a candy factory in Indonesia’s Banten province, killing at least three workers and leaving 36 others unaccounted for, officials said Sunday.
articles.body: JAKARTA, Indonesia — A fire swept through a candy factory in Indonesia’s Banten province, killing at least three workers and leaving 36 others unaccounted for, officials said Sunday. The blaze broke out at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in the Serang district of Banten province, which borders the capital, Jakarta, at 5 p.m. local time on Saturday. Flames engulfed the three-story factory, sending thick black smoke into the sky, television reports showed. Debris littered the floor of the burned-out structure, including twisted metal and blackened, corrugated iron roofing. A company representative said Sunday 300 workers were inside when the blaze started. He added 54 were initially missing, but 15 have since been rescued. The rescued included four injured workers, the National Search and Rescue Agency said in a statement. The remains of the three killed were transferred to a hospital in seven black body bags for identification. The cause of the fire was not immediately known. Survivors said the fire originated from a cooling unit on the third floor, local media reported. Although the blaze had largely been contained as of Sunday, firefighters were still carrying out intensive cooling operations before they could access all parts of the factory, said Tubagus Mahfud, operations chief of the Serang fire department, adding that the remaining hotspots were concentrated in the central and rear sections of the building. “We are conducting sweeps in the areas that have already been brought under control,” Mahfud said. ”Parts of the structure had collapsed, while poor lighting conditions required firefighters to proceed cautiously.” He also said the factory’s production materials could cause the fire to reignite, making it critical to complete cooling operations. Rizky Dwianto, an operations official at the Banten Search and Rescue Agency, said 15 fire trucks, supported by water cannons, were deployed to battle the flames in several parts of the facility more than 12 hours after the fire began. A joint rescue team, including police, the military, the Indonesian Red Cross, and volunteers, was at the scene. “Authorities continue to coordinate with families and the company to determine the whereabouts of employees believed to have been inside the factory when the fire broke out,” he said. Anxious relatives waited for news outside the burnt-out factory. The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products. Indonesia has experienced a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising concerns about workplace safety standards and emergency preparedness at manufacturing facilities.

articles.title: Russian cargo ship still on fire off Finland after drone attack
articles.summary: The ship, bound for Russia’s Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters before drifting into Finnish territory.
articles.body:
A fire on board a Russian cargo ship that was struck by drones off the coast of Finland in the Baltic Sea continued to burn through the night even as efforts were made to douse the flames, the Finnish coastguard said.

Finland’s military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remains at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship.

Pictures and video released by the coastguard on Sunday showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannon overnight to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.

Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwestern coastal region of Leningrad this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland island, the Finnish Defence Forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.

‘War is spilling’ into Finland’s vicinity

Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo suggested the incident was related to Russia’s war on Ukraine.

“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity … Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor,” Orpo said on X.

The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to data from the London Stock Exchange.

The vessel is subject to US sanctions, according to the US Department of the Treasury.

Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Ministry of Defence, according to the company’s website.

articles.title: Man dies in M42 crash near Birmingham Airport
articles.summary: Police confirm a van driver died following a serious crash on the M42 on Saturday.
articles.body:
A man died in a serious crash on the M42 near Birmingham Airport, police said.

The crash, involving a van and a lorry, happened on the northbound carriageway of the motorway between junction 5a and junction six on Saturday, just after 12:30 GMT.

The van driver, a man in his 40s, died at the scene, West Midlands Police said.

The carriageway remained closed for several hours but was fully reopened to traffic earlier on Sunday morning.

Motorists caught in standstill traffic described seeing a "huge fire" a fter the crash, while West Midlands Police urged motorists to avoid the area.

The driver of the lorry remained at the scene and was helping officers with their investigation as inquiries remained ongoing, a spokesperson added.

The force said the van driver's family was told what had happened and specialist officers were offering them support.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene following the crash, National Highways confirmed, while West Midlands Police and West Midlands Fire Service attended.

Overnight resurfacing work was carried out, and officers urged anyone with dashcam footage or information about the crash to contact them.

Sgt Richard Evans said: "We are working to establish exactly how the collision happened and would ask people who were driving on that stretch of the M42 at around 12:30 yesterday to check their dashcam.

"We'd ask that anyone who has footage or any information, and is yet to speak to us, gets in contact."

articles.title: ‘Not everything can happen during elections’: Why Ladakh’s MHA dialogue is on hold till Dec 4
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: The Ladakh administration on Sunday welcomed the high voter turnout in the panchayat and municipal elections held on Saturday, saying it
articles.body: SRINAGAR: The Ladakh administration on Sunday welcomed the high voter turnout in the panchayat and municipal elections held on Saturday, saying it reflected people's desire for democracy.Appealing to residents to participate in large numbers in the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council (LAHDC) elections scheduled for December 4, Ladakh chief secretary Ashish Kundra said talks between leaders of the region and the ministry of home affairs (MHA) would resume after the polls.Addressing a press conference in Leh, Kundra said negotiations should continue and parties should not outrightly reject proposals on the table.He asserted that the government of India was committed to providing the best possible solution under Article 371 for the people of Ladakh. He also urged Leh Apex Body member and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk not to make what he called provocative statements during the election season.“The voter turnout percentage and the fact that people have participated in such large numbers, is a testament to the fact that people in Ladakh want democracy,” Kundra said.Ladakh recorded a 70.03% turnout in the panchayat elections and 52.4% in the municipal council polls on Saturday. “We must not forget that the last panchayat and municipal elections were held in 2018. This is the first time elections are being held since Ladakh became a Union Territory,” he said.On talks between the MHA and Ladakh leaders represented by the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA), Kundra said the dialogue would resume soon after the election process was over.“The dialogue between the ministry of home affairs and the political leadership is a political dialogue. Anything that could influence the outcome of elections cannot be undertaken during the election process,” he said.Kundra said he had personally conveyed to Chering Dorjay Lakrook, co-chairman of the LAB, on two occasions that the MHA would resume political dialogue on the larger structure or body under discussion once the elections were over.He indicated that elected representatives could also be included in the talks alongside the LAB and KDA.“We are not saying that talks with the Leh Apex Body and the Kargil Democratic Alliance will come to an end (after the polls). But those who are elected as representatives are also the voice of the people and they will have to be brought into the dialogue also,” he said.However, he added: “It is incorrect to suggest, as some statements appear to imply, that we will speak only to the elected representatives and leave the LAB and KDA out of the process. Such statements are misleading and create confusion.”Kundra also said a maximalist position should be avoided during negotiations and that dialogue should not be discontinued.“One should never outrightly reject what is on the table. In any kind of negotiation a few things are required. First, mutual trust. Second, a process of give and take. I cannot adopt a maximalist position and say that I want this and only this. We have to accommodate each other,” he said.He reiterated that within the framework of the Constitution of India, the government was committed to providing the best possible solution under Article 371 to Ladakh.Asked about the LAB's demand to defer the LAHDC elections, Kundra said, “Only 10 to 12 days are left for the elections and around 70% of the people have already voted in the Panchayat election. So at this stage, to claim that 40% of the people are not even here is not correct. It is not as if people are casting their votes without being present.”On the demand for polling booths in Srinagar and Jammu for Ladakh residents currently in these cities, he said it would not be possible to arrange them as polling stations had already been frozen.However, he said special arrangements could be explored for those currently outside Ladakh, including facilitating travel through Sadbhavana flights.“I would have no objection to it. But we will have to speak to the Air Force authorities to explore whether special flights can be arranged so that anyone who wishes to vote can travel to Ladakh, cast their vote and then move back,” he said.Stay updated with the latest Srinagar news. articles.title: 6 vintage Thanksgiving recipes of decades past, from oyster stuffing to hot Dr Pepper
articles.summary: Creamed pearl onions, oyster stuffing and mincemeat pie once anchored holiday tables, says one chef, as vintage Thanksgiving recipes fade away.
articles.body: Before today's familiar lineup of Thanksgiving favorites, home cooks served rich and resourceful dishes and drinks that have largely disappeared from the holiday table. While mashed potatoes, green bean casserole and mac and cheese might be some of the most popular dishes to pass around the table today, holiday menus of decades past transformed everyday pantry staples and convenience foods into celebratory recipes. "Older Thanksgiving menus often included dishes such as creamed onions, oyster stuffing and mincemeat pie," Dennis Littley, a New Jersey-based chef and founder of Ask Chef Dennis, told Fox News Digital. FROM FONDUE TO CASSEROLES: CLASSIC 1960S FOODS THAT DEFINED A GENERATION "Some have become less common as tastes and holiday menus have changed, though people still bring them back when they want to revive a family recipe." Here's a look at six vintage recipes, including a warm, spiced soda drink. 1. Creamed pearl onions Creamed pearl onions appeared in cookbooks as far back as 1896, according to online records, and were a familiar addition to Thanksgiving spreads by the 1920s, Taste of Home reported. The dish pairs tender onions with a buttery white sauce similar to French béchamel. Frozen pearl onions later made it easier to prepare. The old-fashioned side still has devoted fans, according to Bon Appétit. Chef Thomas Keller has said his mother's creamed onions are a Thanksgiving dish he "can't live without." 5 FORGOTTEN ICE CREAM FLAVORS FROM THE '70S THAT FANS ARE BEGGING TO BE BROUGHT BACK In a Reddit thread dedicated to old recipes, one person said his or her family still makes creamed onions today, carrying on a tradition from the person's great-grandmother. 2. Oyster stuffing or dressing Oyster dressing called for combining shucked oysters and their brine with classic stuffing ingredients including bread, celery and spices. It was a Thanksgiving staple in the 1800s, when oysters were regularly available for purchase from refrigerated railcars, Food52 reported. 6 ICONIC AMERICAN RESTAURANTS STILL SERVING UP NOSTALGIA AND CLASSIC FLAVORS The dish, with roots in British culinary traditions, fell out of favor in the Northeast as oyster populations declined and tastes shifted toward ingredients such as sausage. 3. Mincemeat pie Before pumpkin and apple pie solidified their place at the table, there was a meaty dessert contender. The filling of mincemeat pie was originally a sweet and savory mix of dried fruit, spices, citrus and meat — often beef or mutton — with suet, the fat of the meat. "When we were kids my mom would always do mincemeat pie for both Thanksgiving and Christmas and we hated it," one commenter on Reddit recalled. THANKSGIVING DINNER KITS: 7 GROCERY CHAINS OFFERING HOLIDAY MEALS FOR UNDER $70 Over time, meat disappeared from many recipes, leaving only the richly spiced fruit filling behind, though the pie's name still hints at its historic roots. 4. Aspic Long before Jell-O, cooks prepared savory aspics by simmering collagen-rich bones, skin and feet until the broth set, according to the Michelin Guide. A labor-intensive showpiece once common in upscale French cuisine and wealthy households, aspic became more accessible with commercial gelatin and home refrigeration. By the mid-20th century, savory molds filled with meat, seafood, vegetables or hard-boiled eggs became a fashionable centerpiece at gatherings. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Aspics have made a recent comeback as home cooks explore nostalgic dishes and fine-dining chefs reimagine them as edible art, Fox News Digital previously reported. 5. Cranberry Surprise The mayonnaise company Hellmann's promoted this molded holiday gelatin "salad" in a 1958 ad, according to reports. Made with cranberry sauce, gelatin, mayonnaise, fruit and nuts, "Cranberry Souffle Salad" was chilled, whipped until fluffy and served on lettuce. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ A separate 1960 Hellmann's ad featured cranberry "candles," made with a similar mixture, molded in juice cans and topped with lit birthday candles, Bon Appétit reported. 6. Hot Dr Pepper CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES In the 1950s and 1960s, Dr Pepper promoted the hot winter beverage, which called for heating the soda up to approximately 180 degrees Fahrenheit and then pouring it over a slice of lemon, as a way to boost sales during the slower winter months. The idea originated in September 1958, when company president Wesby R. Parker visited a bottling plant during a blizzard and a salesman joked that they needed a hot beverage to sell during cold weather, according to the Dr Pepper Museum. articles.title: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
articles.summary: Tehran has ramped up attacks as the US naval blockade and sanctions campaign hurt the country economically.
articles.body:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have targeted radars at a United States military base in Bahrain, as Iran has intensified attacks over the past week, hitting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, and downing US drones.

At least 25 tankers have been hit in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes, in the past seven days, causing the Gulf oil flow to drop sharply.

The escalating attacks come as Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country is facing what he called a “silent economic war” amid US sanctions and a naval blockade.

So what is behind Iran’s latest escalation, and will it trigger a new round of hostilities between Tehran and Washington or force the two sides to sit down for talks to end the war that has caused a global energy crisis?

Bahrain has faced the brunt of Iran’s attacks in recent days.

On Saturday, Manama said an Iranian strike hit a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire , as it thwarted several other attacks that day.

The IRGC said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting US military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, claiming to have destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.

Iranian state media reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain crashed on Sitra Island near Manama, sparking a large fire.

The IRGC said the operation was retaliation for a US strike on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island. Iran has justified the attacks as a response to continued violations of its airspace, including by US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones.

Bahrain has faced three drone attacks in recent days after a lull in fighting for several weeks.

Iran’s army on Saturday said its air defences fired a missile at a US F-16 jet over the Gulf the previous evening, damaging the aircraft, the IRNA news agency reported. However, US Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, stating that “all US fighter jets in the Middle East are safe and accounted for”.

Iranian forces on Sunday also said they shot down another MQ-1 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC claimed it was the 20th US drone of this type to be shot down since the war began in late February and the fourth in the past 24 hours.

Meanwhile, British maritime authorities reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz near Oman.

Al Jazeera correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week, with about 25 since November 14.

Last week, the Iranian army also said it targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem base. The attack came after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which remains under effective Iranian control.

How are attacks affecting oil exports through Hormuz?

Oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz has seen a considerable dip as Iran has escalated attacks on a near-daily basis.

According to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), 263 ships passed through the key waterway between November 12 and 18, which is 15 percent fewer than the previous week and 20 percent fewer than the week before that.

Of those vessels, 37 were oil tankers, down from 52 the previous week, UKMTO reported on Friday.

The figures, however, could be higher as vessels passing through as part of shadow fleets are not officially registered.

About 135 ships passed daily through the vital strait before the war began in February.

Last week, the US maritime agency warned that the Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums, with insurance rates up from 0.10-0.25 percent before the war to 3.5-7.5 percent.

Oil prices have spiked, crossing $100 a barrel before settling down to $83, still more than $15 from before the war.

Cumulative losses from the conflict have now reached 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas supply from the Gulf, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.

The IEA, however, added that the conflict could cut world oil demand by more than 4 percent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response.

As Iran has ramped up attacks, senior officials have asked the US to choose between surrendering to missiles or to diplomacy.

The attacks indicate that Iran is using its leverage in the conflict, sending the message that the US allies in the region will continue to bear the brunt of its actions if the war does not end.

The attacks aim to diminish US military capabilities in the region and “also to spread the pain of the war widely to include the entire [Gulf region] and, indirectly, global economies via higher shipping costs and stressed supplies of essentials”, Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, told Al Jazeera.

The single biggest driver of this strategy, Khouri said, is for Iran to continually ensure that it will no longer “suffer alone from US-Israel-imperial assaults”.

Tehran is hoping to change US policy by revealing its inability to protect its own facilities or those of its Arab allies, which could prompt Arab governments to press US President Donald Trump to end the war, Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, added.

Meanwhile, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told Iranian media that he considers the economic blockade imposed by the US on Iran an act of war.

“We consider the economic siege a hostile act, and we will take any necessary measures to break this economic siege,” Gharibabadi told Iranian reporters.

The ongoing US naval blockade on Iran, overland trade disruptions and a wave of new sanctions imposed in August as part of Operation Economic Outcast are hurting Iran economically.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has led Washington’s sanctions regime against Tehran, has claimed the economic embargo will result in a 25 percent contraction of the Iranian economy by the year ending March 2027.

However, Iranian authorities insist they can withstand the economic pressure.

The strikes on US interests in the Gulf in recent days have therefore been viewed as a defiant response to the US campaign. But there are signs that the country’s economy and common Iranians are suffering from the current conditions.

Could there be renewed military confrontation?

Trump may choose to declare victory and walk away from the war on Iran rather than negotiate a deal, but continuing the naval blockade on Iran would risk further military escalation, says Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Parsi said Trump was unlikely to accept an agreement that could be seen in Washington as showing the war had failed.

“If he continues the blockade, there will be escalation,” Parsi warned, arguing that Iran would not refrain from retaliating against continued economic pressure.

He said Trump would need to “slowly, perhaps imperceptibly, lift the blockade, as well as lift some of the sanctions” if he wanted to withdraw from the confrontation without renewed fighting.

Hassan Ahmadian, professor at the University of Tehran, said Iran is forcing a “binary” choice on Trump.

If Washington lets the tankers pass, the US blockade “ends without an agreement or war”, Ahmadian said on X. However, if the US attacks the vessels, it could face “Iranian responses that will be difficult for [Trump] to avoid”.

Trump said on Saturday he had plans to make a deal with Iran that is “permanent” and prevents it from getting a nuclear weapon.

He also told US broadcaster Fox News that he was never very interested in regime change in Iran, but called its new leadership “more rational”.

articles.title: Blanchelande College wins mental health and wellbeing award
articles.summary: The opening of a wellbeing room for students at Blanchelande College is recognised by judges.
articles.body:
A school has received recognition for helping support the mental health of pupils.

Blanchelande College in St Andrews, Guernsey, won the Mental Health and Wellbeing Award at the 2026 Independent Schools Association Awards earlier this week.

The independent Catholic school for boys and girls was recognised for its Emmaus Space, a wellbeing room that opened in September 2025.

It was also commended for a drop in school refusal, a rise in attendance and providing a comprehensive network of care.

School leaders said the award reflected their belief in education that develops pupils academically, socially, emotionally and spiritually.

Vice principal Dr Vanessa Mitchell said: "We are incredibly proud to receive this award.

"It recognises our whole college community's commitment to ensuring every child feels seen, heard, understood and supported."

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack several Palestinian villages in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: Attacks in Ramallah, el-Bireh provinces included the burning of 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on homes.
articles.body:
Israeli settlers have attacked several Palestinian towns and villages in the central occupied West Bank, burning cars and damaging property.

The attacks early on Sunday included the burning of 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on the walls of homes in Ramallah and el-Bireh provinces, reported the Palestinian news agency Wafa. The incidents were reported in Kafr Malik village, Deir Abu Mash’al village, and Deir al-Sudan village.

“Residents were awakened around two in the morning by sounds of fire and explosions. They realised the settlers had set fire to cars,” reported Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh from Kafr Malik.

Israeli settler violence has surged across the occupied West Bank since Israel launched its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza. At least 1,222 people, including 255 children, have been killed in attacks there since Israel launched its war in October 2023 in response to the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.

The Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said there was a significant increase in the number of attacks throughout the Palestinian territory last month.

According to the Palestinian Authority body, there were 3,133 attacks in October, with Israeli forces responsible for 1,764 of them and Israeli settlers 1,369.

The commission said the total number of attacks increased by 53 percent compared with September when 2,051 attacks were recorded. Settler attacks alone rose from 647 in September to 1,369 in October – a 112 percent increase.

Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar Party, who has been tasked with forming a new government after Israel’s general election last month, criticised the latest attacks on Sunday.

He wrote on social media that the attacks were “Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word, and it must be called what it is”.

“Sabotage by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermines regional stability, endangers lives and severely damages the national security of the state of Israel and its foreign relations,” he posted on X.

“The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy,” he added, referring to far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

Ben-Gvir rejected the allegations and said Eisenkot was rushing to conclusions. He wrote on social media that Eisenkot’s stance represents a “down payment” to Arab Knesset member Ahmad Tibi in preparation for forming a government with the support of Arab parties.

Settlers are often “escorted by Israeli squads and they do nothing to stop the attackers,” Shai Parnes of the Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem told Al Jazeera.

The Israeli military said it was sending police officers and investigators from the Criminal Identification Unit to the attacked areas “to collect evidence as part of the ongoing investigation”, the military wrote on social media.
